cardyiq.name: Cardy
cardyiq.tagline: A sports network in Iraq for individual visits and monthly memberships at partner venues.
cardyiq.summary: I joined Cardy a few days after launch as a consultant to give technical advice. Over the following year, my role grew into business, product and engineering work. I built the technical team first and rebuilt the dashboard. We introduced a new business model in the existing app before I led the Flutter rewrite, keeping the same features in the new interface. The backend came last, moving from PHP and MySQL to Bun and PostgreSQL. Along the way, I rebuilt the website and introduced new features. What interests me about Cardy is connecting sports and technology through good apps.
stack: Redis for caching and background work

sections.heading: How Cardy works
sections.lede: Choose a venue, arrive and scan its Cardy QR code.
sections.body:
Members choose a partner gym, pool, padel court or another sports venue in the app. When they arrive, they find the special Cardy QR code and scan it to check in. They can pay for individual visits with prepaid points or subscribe to a monthly membership at one venue.

The app is available in Arabic, English and Kurdish.

sections.heading: How does Cardy work for partners?
sections.lede: The dashboard brings bookings, visits and payments into one place.
sections.body: Venue owners use the dashboard to manage their venue information, pricing, memberships and bookings. They can follow visits and member activity, review payments and use settlement reports. The dashboard is in Arabic, matching the language they use in their daily work.

sections.heading: Where I started
sections.lede: The product was live. It was not ready.
sections.body: I joined as a consultant a few days after launch. People were already using Cardy, so I had to understand what was getting in their way. The work soon grew beyond simple technical advice.
bullets: A DNS/CDN problem made the app unreachable on Iraqi networks. People were being told to install a VPN to use it.
The Laravel and MySQL backend was full of spaghetti code, making even small changes impossible.
There was no CI/CD and no caching. Deployments were painful, so they rarely happened.
Payments were cash only. Someone had to collect money from every venue.
The dashboard was in English, while the people using it every day spoke Arabic.
The business model was the biggest problem. Entry passes limited the sports, venues and pricing Cardy could support.

sections.heading: Building the team and how we work
sections.body:
I built the technical team first. Over the following year, that gave us the people to rebuild the dashboard and app, introduce new features and eventually replace the backend. I still work in the code, but leading the team also means giving people enough context to own their part of the product.

Across this work, I introduced CI/CD and separate development, testing and production environments on Dokploy. Changes go through testing and review before release. Translation and configuration checks are automated, so the same issues do not depend on someone remembering to look for them every time. Monitoring and backups are part of the setup too.

I keep product requirements, technical overviews and release instructions with the work. Larger features get a review that challenges the assumptions before we ship them.

sections.heading: A dashboard for the people using it
sections.lede: An English template was the wrong starting point for a team working in Arabic.
sections.body:
After building the team, I rebuilt the dashboard. The first version used a purchased React admin template. It was English only, and the home screen showed three visitor counters. Venue owners and the operations team worked in Arabic every day, so I rebuilt it from the ground up with React 19, TypeScript, TanStack, shadcn/ui and Tailwind, using a right to left layout from the start.

I added search, filters, exports and settlement reports around the work the team actually does. We use the Arabic labels in our requirements too, so the engineers and operators can discuss the same task in the same words.

sections.heading: Changing the business model before the UI
sections.body:
Entry passes had limited the sports, venues and prices Cardy could support, so we decided to change the business model to prepaid points and monthly memberships. Members would be able to pay for individual visits across partner venues or choose a monthly plan for one venue.

Members already knew their way around the old interface, even with its problems. From previous experience, I knew that changing the business model and the interface at the same time would ask them to learn too much at once. I brought that experience to Cardy, and we introduced the new model and its features in the familiar interface first.

Payments needed attention too. Before I joined, they were cash only. I brought the gateways behind one payment layer so the app uses the same flow regardless of the provider. The backend checks payment confirmation and repeated requests before crediting points, because a retry must not add the same points twice.

Alongside the product changes, I stabilised the inherited system and moved Cardy to hosting that worked on Iraqi networks, resolving the DNS/CDN problem that had led people to be told to install a VPN.

sections.heading: Rebuilding the app with familiar features
sections.body:
After introducing the new business model, I led the Flutter app rewrite. We changed the UI while keeping exactly the same features, so members could use the product they already knew in a new interface.

Only after that did we introduce new features in the rebuilt app, such as member challenges. The sequence mattered to me. Changing the model, rebuilding the UI and adding features were separate steps, each giving people one change to understand at a time.

sections.heading: Explaining Cardy on the website
sections.lede: The public site needed to catch up with the product.
sections.body:
The old website was a WordPress and Elementor homepage in English. I rebuilt it as a static Astro site with Arabic in Iraqi dialect as the main language, alongside English and Kurdish Sorani. It explains the visit and membership options, shows real venues on the map and sends each visitor to the right app store.

I also introduced a Cardy for Partners page to explain how Cardy works for venue owners. It covers the venue setup, dashboard and cost, with a form to join Cardy.

I organised the translations by language and added checks for missing text. The site also includes the privacy, terms and account deletion pages the app needs. A static build suited this work, and it follows the same testing and release process as the rest of Cardy.

sections.heading: From PHP and MySQL to Bun and PostgreSQL
sections.lede: I had to migrate an awful backend and database structure.
sections.body:
The backend rebuild came last, after the team, dashboard and app. I moved it from PHP and MySQL to Bun and PostgreSQL, but wanted more than a change of language. Before writing the replacement, I documented the data model, migration steps, risks and a way back if the change did not go as planned. The existing app was still in use, so I rebuilt one area at a time.

I captured sanitised examples from the Laravel API and built a tool that sent the same request to both backends. It compared the response status, structure, types and side effects. That gave me a concrete way to decide whether each area was ready, including the awkward cases a rewrite can easily miss.

The data migration had its own checks. Row totals, points and balances had to reconcile before a run counted as complete. I rehearsed the migration and wrote down the release and rollback steps, so moving to the new backend was something we could review and repeat.

items.title: Test the behaviour that matters
items.text: Alongside unit tests, I used integration tests with PostgreSQL and Redis for scans, bookings and credits. Concurrent requests and repeated actions were part of those checks.

items.title: Measure before tuning
items.text: Load tests found a bottleneck in the venue detail route, which I addressed with response caching. I also accounted for members sharing a carrier IP on local mobile networks.

items.title: Leave a backend people can understand
items.text: The API, worker and scheduler share one codebase, with OpenAPI documentation generated from the code. That helps the team follow the system as it changes.

sections.heading: What I take from Cardy
sections.body:
Cardy has reached 20K downloads, 200 sports venues and 2,000 subscribers. I'm proud of the work I've contributed with the team over the year, from building the team itself to rebuilding the dashboard, app and backend, and changing the model those systems support.

The work connected business, product and engineering. The entry pass model, the language of the dashboard and the way we released changes all needed attention. Previous experience helped me decide how to introduce those changes, including keeping the business model change separate from the new app UI. Connecting sports and technology through good apps meant working through all of those decisions. The backend rewrite was one part of a much larger change.

qi-card.name: Qi
qi-card.tagline: Qi is Iraq’s largest e-payments company. Millions of people get paid, pay bills and send money through Qi cards and the SuperQi app.
qi-card.summary: I'm a software engineer at Qi, working across billing and acquiring (B2B collection). I build mini-apps inside SuperQi, where people find bills, manage their shops and apply for housing loans. I also work on the internal tools used behind the scenes.
stack: QiNeo and Alipay Plus native DSL target

sections.heading: My part in the work
sections.body:
Across projects, I worked with the business team to shape requirements, then agreed the technical approach with my manager, a solution architect. I collaborated with UI/UX, backend, DevOps and information security teams to carry the work forward. I also worked with the Alipay team at Ant Group and Qi's international teams in Germany and India, including payment work aligned with ISO 8583 and secure application development guided by ISO/IEC 27034.

That work spanned Tasdid+, Tasdid Merchant, Jabi+, Basmayah, Qi Hawala and other products. My contribution differed by project: I started Tasdid+ from an empty template using the design team's work, built Basmayah's front end in three days from a teammate's designs and UX specification, and developed features in Jabi+ and Tasdid Merchant. On Qi Hawala, I set up the foundation while a teammate built most of the screens. These were team efforts; each story below describes the part I owned.

asheerty.name: Asheerty
asheerty.tagline: An Arabic family tree app. Build your family’s tree with your relatives, keep every person’s story, and order it as a framed poster.
asheerty.summary: I built Asheerty on my own, from the iOS and Android app to the backend, website and dashboard with a custom editor for laying out each family tree poster. The work goes beyond the app. I also built a WhatsApp support assistant and a private video studio for making its ads. What connects all of it is the family tree, keeping it editable on a phone and turning it into artwork people can put on their wall.
stack: Shopify React Native Skia, Reanimated, Zustand and TanStack Query
OpenAI vision for the AI Tree Builder
React, Vite, TanStack Router, Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui
WaSphere and n8n for WhatsApp support
Bun, Hono, Drizzle and ComfyUI for Studio
Claude Code and Codex as build tools

sections.heading: From a family record to a living tree
sections.lede: Asheerty is for families whose history is still on paper or in one person's memory.
sections.body:
A family starts with one name and adds relatives, photos, dates and their stories. Others can join through a shared link to look at the tree or help build it. I made the app in Arabic, with right-to-left layouts from the beginning, rather than treating the language as something to add later.

The tree can stay in the app, but it can also become a framed poster. Each framed poster has a QR code that opens the same living tree, keeping the artwork connected to the family's record. This is why I built the mobile app, poster editor and order process together.

sections.heading: Making a large family tree usable
sections.body:
A tree is useful only if people can find their way around it. I built a canvas with pan, zoom and collapsible branches, using Shopify's React Native Skia to draw the connections and render only what's in view. There is also a card view and search for someone who wants to find a person without exploring the whole diagram.

Adding a relative opens an editor for their name, relationship, life dates, photos and story. Quick additions help a family grow the tree gradually, and an offline queue keeps edits made without a connection. Relatives can propose changes, which the owner reviews before accepting them. The tree can be shared without giving everyone the same editing access.

sections.heading: Bringing an old paper tree into the app
sections.lede: The AI Tree Builder reads a photograph, but the family still checks the result.
sections.body:
Asking a family to type out a tree they already have on paper creates a lot of repeated work. I built an import flow where they photograph the chart and tap its root. The backend uses OpenAI vision to read names and notes, map the relationships and reconstruct a draft tree.

One pass is not enough to trust the result. A separate review looks for missed people and branches, and server checks catch broken links and cycles before the draft reaches the app. Uncertain names and relationships stay marked for review. AI helps with the transcription, while the family remains responsible for deciding what is correct.

sections.heading: Turning the tree into a poster
sections.lede: The mobile app collects the order. The dashboard is where I prepare the artwork.
sections.body:
The print flow lets a customer choose the size, frame, copies and recipients, then follow the order from preview to delivery. Behind that flow, I built an Arabic dashboard and a poster editor that works in centimetres. The tree, frame, background, QR code and notes all belong to the same layout.

The editor can draw the family as branches and leaves, concentric rings or cards connected from top to bottom. I added generated variations, alignment tools, clash warnings, undo and redo, and saved snapshots so a layout can be worked on without losing earlier decisions. It exports SVG, HTML, PDF and PNG, and sends a watermarked preview to the customer's app.

Nothing goes to print before the customer accepts the preview and the first payment is confirmed. Each order keeps its approved artwork, including for a reprint. Version checks prevent a stale save from overwriting a newer layout, and the dashboard offers only the action that belongs to the order's current stage.

sections.heading: Keeping the app and the business connected
sections.body:
I built the API with TypeScript on Bun, Express, Prisma and PostgreSQL. It handles family records, photos, shared trees and print orders. Redis provides caching, MinIO stores photos and assets, and NotifyX handles push notifications. These pieces support the same journey, from adding a relative to receiving a poster.

Shared links also need to work outside the app. I made readable share pages with a title and image for WhatsApp and Facebook, and an invitation page that opens the tree or sends a relative to the right app store. The Arabic website includes a sample tree people can try in their browser. I also connected campaign links and Android install attribution to account creation so I can follow where sign-ups come from.

I maintain both native projects, use Fastlane for store uploads and host the app's JavaScript update service myself. Backend tests cover the API, while health checks and metrics help me operate it after release.

sections.heading: Handling support without guessing
sections.body:
I built a WhatsApp assistant with n8n on top of WaSphere, an open source WhatsApp gateway. My work includes hosting the gateway, updating its WhatsApp engine, fixing video message handling and building the assistant around it.

The assistant answers questions about Asheerty in the customer's language, including Iraqi Arabic. It does not invent account, payment or order information. When a question needs private information or a person, it hands the conversation over and stays quiet. Message tracking prevents duplicate replies, and delivery records let me see whether a response was actually sent. This gives routine questions an answer while keeping a person involved where the assistant cannot know enough.

sections.heading: Building tools for the work around the product
sections.body:
Making the app also meant making its marketing videos. I built Studio in a week in September 2026, using two Windows PCs of my own to run render jobs through ComfyUI. From the browser I can write a brief, add image and audio references, send a job and follow its progress.

A Director flow breaks a storyboard into clips with timing, narration and references. I review those clips before rendering them, and finished clips can be assembled into one MP4 in the browser with ffmpeg.wasm. A separate pipeline makes short tutorial videos from HTML pages and checks their text placement before encoding.

Studio and the support assistant are part of the same work as the app and poster editor. Building Asheerty on my own has meant building the tools I need to explain it, support it and keep it running.

sections.heading: What the printed product changes
sections.body: A bug on a screen can be fixed with an update. A mistake that has been printed, framed and shipped costs real money. That made review part of the product, from checking an imported family tree to approving the final artwork. The app keeps the family record alive, while the order process makes sure the version that leaves the printer is the one the customer accepted.

notifyx.name: NotifyX
notifyx.tagline: The notification system I built once and keep using across my projects.
notifyx.summary: I built NotifyX because notifications kept becoming another system to rebuild in every app. It brings the providers, worker, scheduler and delivery history together, so I can add notifications early and spend my time on the product itself. I built the API, dashboard and client SDKs, and made the project open source.
stack: Web, Flutter and React Native SDKs
FCM, APNS, HMS and Web Push

sections.heading: Why I built it
sections.body:
I kept rebuilding notifications for every project I worked on. Between setting up providers, workers and scheduling, they took time and usually became an afterthought. Web notifications were even easier to forget.

So I built NotifyX once and started using it across my projects. It has its own worker and scheduler, which makes notifications easy to set up from day zero, even for an MVP. The best part is that it's open source, so anyone can adapt it to their own needs.

sections.heading: Building the reusable part
sections.body:
I built the API, queue, workers and scheduler with Node.js, BullMQ, Redis, PostgreSQL and Prisma. FCM, APNS, HMS and Web Push sit behind the same API, so each app doesn't need its own implementation for every provider. I also wrote SDKs for web, Flutter and React Native.

Immediate messages and scheduled campaigns use the same delivery pipeline. That let me keep the repeated infrastructure in NotifyX rather than adding a separate worker and scheduler to each product.

sections.heading: Making delivery visible
sections.body:
Sending a message is only part of the work. A provider can time out, a device token can become invalid, or a worker can stop during a job. I added retries with backoff, removal of invalid tokens and a place to inspect permanent failures. Delivery states stay in PostgreSQL, and the React dashboard makes them visible without searching through logs.

The dashboard also brings together message composition, campaigns, reusable templates and application configuration. These are the tools I need around the delivery system to keep using it across different apps.

sections.heading: What it became
sections.body:
I started building it in 2024 while exploring what AI could help me do. Building a complete system with it felt amazing back then. I've been using NotifyX across multiple apps since, and I'm proud of how well it's held up. It just works.

Cardyiq, Sadeek, Asheerty, Orivo and Baseerah use NotifyX. Having this part ready has made it easier to include notifications at the beginning of a new project, rather than waiting until everything else is finished.

sections.heading: What I'd improve next
sections.body: I'd add per-application rate limits earlier, so a busy app has less effect on the others sharing a deployment. I'd also define delivery receipts more clearly from the start. Building something reusable means paying attention to what happens when several products depend on it, not just getting the first message sent.

sadeek.name: Sadeek
sadeek.tagline: A Telegram bot for sellers. Send it one photo and it cleans the image, writes the description, suggests a price and publishes the listing to an e-store.
sadeek.summary: I built and operated Sadeek on my own, from the Telegram bot and image processing to the storefront and paid usage. It reached more than 10,000 users and handled more than 150,000 AI requests.
stack: n8n for the original processing workflow
React Native and Expo for the unreleased app
Background removal, relighting and AI try-on

sections.heading: Starting with a photo
sections.lede: Sellers had rough phone photos and no laptops. Sadeek uses AI to clean each image and create a complete listing for any product.
sections.body:
Putting a listing together still meant cleaning up the image, writing a description and deciding on a price. They already used Telegram, so I built the product there. A seller could send a photo and continue in the same conversation while Sadeek prepared the listing.

I built the whole product myself, including the bot, processing workflow, storefront and day to day operation. The storefront gave sellers somewhere to publish the result.

sections.heading: Connecting the work behind the chat
sections.body:
A useful listing needed more than a single model response. I connected background removal, relighting and AI try-on with descriptions, price estimates and moderation. The original workflow ran in n8n, with GPT and Gemini handling the content, pricing and moderation work.

I split processing into stages so I could check the result, retry a failed step and improve it without starting the whole request again. The bot also had to remember where each seller was in the conversation. Receiving a new photo, waiting for a result and managing an existing listing needed different responses.

items.title: Prepare the product image
items.text: The input was often an ordinary phone photo. Image cleanup was part of preparing a listing, alongside the written content.

items.title: Review before publication
items.text: I put moderation between generation and publication so the storefront would not publish every model response automatically.

items.title: Keep the flow inside Telegram
items.text: I added request history, usage balances and subscription flows so sellers could follow their work and manage usage in the chat.

sections.heading: From n8n to a complete backend
sections.body:
The next step was moving the proven n8n workflow into a complete backend that could handle the full product. It took a seller from a Telegram conversation through image cleanup, AI generated content and pricing, moderation, payment and a published storefront listing.

I built it with grammY, Bun and Express, backed by PostgreSQL, Redis and BullMQ. I separated conversation state, photo processing, payments and search into stages, so I could retry or improve one part without restarting the whole request.

Model routing, batching, caching and fallback providers helped keep paid API costs manageable and gave sellers a clear outcome when a service failed.

sections.heading: Giving the listings a home
sections.body:
I built a Next.js storefront where buyers could browse the generated listings, search for a product and open a seller's store. Product pages brought the images, description, price and seller information together. I also adapted those pages for people browsing from a phone.

The storefront was the publishing part of the same workflow, rather than a separate product sellers had to fill in again. The archived screens below use demo listings.

sections.heading: The app I built after the bot
sections.lede: The Telegram product was released. The later mobile app never shipped to the app stores.
sections.body:
I built the mobile version with React Native and Expo around an Arabic interface and right to left layout, with English and Kurdish translations as well. Sellers could select up to five photos and choose content generation, image editing or product identification. The app followed the queued work until the request succeeded or failed.

I also built product management, seller stores, a points wallet, price feedback, buyer and seller chat, and push notifications. Plan cards and splash screens could be configured from the backend without a new app release. The mobile screens shown here are from that unreleased version and use demo data.

sections.heading: What I take from Sadeek
sections.body:
Sadeek reached more than 10,000 users and handled more than 150,000 AI requests. It gave me experience building and operating an AI product on my own, where the cost of a request, the quality of the input and what happened when processing failed all mattered.

The project is neglected now. If I returned to it, I would decide earlier whether I was building a daily tool for individual sellers or a service other commerce platforms could integrate. I would choose the service for other platforms, set a cost budget for each request and introduce paid usage earlier. Free use helped me understand demand, but told me less about what people were willing to pay for.

hawsr.name: HAWSR
hawsr.tagline: Walkable 3D property tours that open from a link. Clients explore rooms on any device, check floor plans, measure real dimensions and view the space in English, Arabic or Kurdish. Built for real estate developers, agencies and brokers selling property before a visit or before the building exists.
hawsr.summary: HAWSR began as my master's thesis: sharing 3D Revit information in the cloud so all project stakeholders could follow updates and construction changes. The thesis idea was not the product the market was ready to buy, so I pivoted to link-based property tours for real estate developers, agencies and brokers as Iraq's market boomed. I rebuilt the stack while learning by doing, and the new direction found demand in its first year. I sold and delivered tours, led a team of six and closed the business in 2024.

sections.heading: The thesis: sharing Revit information
sections.lede: I wanted every project stakeholder to see the same 3D information and follow changes in the cloud.
sections.body: I was working as an architect and learning to code when I began my Erasmus Mundus master's thesis in Ljubljana. The thesis explored an automation that sent 3D models from Revit to a cloud platform, where all stakeholders could share project information and track construction changes. That was the original HAWSR idea. It addressed a real coordination problem, but it was not the product the market was ready to buy.

sections.heading: The pivot to property tours
sections.lede: I shifted from sharing construction information to helping people understand a property before they visited.
sections.body: As Iraq's real estate market boomed, I saw a clearer opportunity with real estate developers, agencies and brokers. They needed a way to show buyers a property before a visit, or before the building existed. I pivoted HAWSR into a link-based 3D viewer that opened in the browser. The new direction found paying demand in its first year.

sections.heading: A property tour from a link
sections.lede: Buyers could explore a property on the device they already had.
sections.body: A client shared a link, and buyers could walk through rooms on a phone, tablet or laptop. They could switch between a first-person walkthrough, a dollhouse view and a floor plan, then measure real dimensions inside the model. The interface worked in English, Arabic and Kurdish, with no app or headset to install. For a property still being planned, I built the tour from its Revit model; for an existing property, it began with capture and modelling.

sections.heading: Rebuilding the product as I learned
sections.lede: The pivot changed the audience and meant rebuilding the stack around the viewer.
sections.body: I carried the Revit model pipeline forward, then learned by doing as I rebuilt the product for interactive property tours. I moved the viewer to React Three Fiber and added room navigation, floor-plan and dollhouse views, measurement tools and annotations. A Django backend stored projects and tours and delivered model assets to the browser. I also explored 360-degree capture, but kept it as research until the quality and business case were ready.

sections.heading: A first year with real demand
sections.lede: The property-tour pivot succeeded in its first year.
sections.body: We sold and delivered about $60K in tours to multiple clients, including DAMAC for a luxury project in Baghdad. I built and led a team of six. HAWSR won first prize at The Station Foundation incubator, and I presented it to more than 1,000 people. Selling and delivering tours taught me to listen to customers, make product decisions and build the work around a service people would pay for.

sections.heading: Closing the business
sections.lede: A successful first year did not guarantee a market large enough to sustain the company.
sections.body: There were not enough customers to keep growing the team, funding had run out, and the 360-degree capture work was not ready to sell. In 2024, I handed off client work, archived the original pipeline and closed the business. HAWSR taught me to test technical feasibility, customer demand and market size as separate questions.

maaahr.name: Maaahr
maaahr.tagline: An AI interview platform in Arabic and English. Job seekers practice with an interviewer that listens and gives feedback, and hiring teams send candidates a link and get a structured evaluation back.
maaahr.summary: I built Maaahr to help me practice for interviews, then published it so others could answer interview questions, have a conversation and review feedback afterwards. It began as my AI Engineering course capstone project and grew into four connected apps for job seekers and hiring teams. I built it end to end, including the interview, the practice app, the hiring dashboard and the website.
stack: OpenAI Realtime API and Gemini Live for voice interviews

sections.heading: From a capstone to a conversation
sections.lede: Interview advice is easy to read and harder to put into practice.
sections.body: Maaahr started as a text based AI Engineering capstone. I wanted to make interview practice easier to do, especially when finding someone to practise with was difficult. During a hackathon, I rebuilt the interview around the OpenAI Realtime API so it could listen and speak. I kept building around that conversation, adding a place to choose a role, practise again and see what needed work.

sections.heading: Practising for an actual role
sections.body: The practice app lets someone choose a position from a library or describe their own. The interview uses that role's description, experience level and focus areas to guide the questions. They can answer through text or voice, then review a summary, strengths and feedback on each answer. I kept previous attempts under the same position so candidates could compare sessions and see how their answers changed.

items.title: Arabic and English throughout
items.text: I built Arabic and English into the questions, prompts, interfaces, reports and emails. The app supports right-to-left and left-to-right layouts, helping job seekers prepare for interviews in either language, as the market requires.

items.title: A clear start
items.text: The interview app introduces the session, explains the available answer formats and timing, then brings the candidate into the conversation.

sections.heading: Using the same interview for hiring
sections.body: I also built a workflow for hiring teams around the same interview. A company creates a position with its questions, focus areas and time limits, then shares a link with candidates. The dashboard brings the responses together, with a summary and feedback for each candidate. This gave the product two different entry points while keeping the interview and its results connected.

sections.heading: Making voice feel like a conversation
sections.lede: Voice practice should feel like a real exchange.
sections.body: I shaped the interview so candidates could focus on their answers, not the screen. Clear cues show when the interviewer is speaking and when it is their turn. A pause to think still feels like part of the conversation, and the exchange keeps its rhythm from the first question to the last.

items.title: The same path to feedback
items.text: I saved the interviewer's transcript as a question and the candidate's transcript as an answer. Text and voice sessions could then use the same feedback flow, result page and email.

sections.heading: What I built and what remains
sections.body: Between December 2024 and August 2025, I took Maaahr from a text capstone to four connected apps with voice interviews. The screenshots show the interfaces with sample data and a demo session. The lesson I took from it was how much voice depends on timing. Connecting an audio model was only part of making the interview feel natural.

items.title: What I'd work on next
items.text: I'd add recording and review so people could hear an answer beside its feedback. I'd also explore different interviewer styles and compare the scoring with real hiring decisions. The score is a part of the product I would still want to calibrate.

tasdid.name: Tasdid+
tasdid.tagline: Tasdid is Qi's bill platform in Iraq: billers and merchants issue invoices, customers are notified and can pay from the Qi wallet. Tasdid+ is its mini-app inside SuperQi, and I built it.
tasdid.summary: I worked on releasing the Tasdid mini-app for SuperQi, collaborating with the business, UI/UX, backend, DevOps and information security teams. I aligned requirements with my manager, a solution architect. After launch, I added Auto-debt subscriptions, direct pay, money requests and quick merchant invoicing.

sections.heading: What Tasdid is
sections.lede: One place for every bill.
sections.body:
Tasdid (tasdid.net) is Qi Card's platform for issuing and paying bills electronically. A biller or merchant creates a single invoice or uploads a whole batch, customises it and sends it. The customer gets a notification when the bill is issued and again when it is paid, and pays from the Qi wallet, by QR, or in the app. Electricity, water, internet, residential compounds, schools, merchants and government agencies use it for billing. Tasdid+ also supports peer-to-peer money requests.

Tasdid+ is the customer-facing mini-app inside SuperQi, Qi's super-app built with Ant International on Alipay+ technology. Everything on this page is that mini-app.

sections.heading: What I built
bullets: The mini-app itself. Since February 2026, I have written its routing, state, API layer and pages. About 80% of its commits are mine; the UI design came from Qi's design team.
Bill lookup and payment: categories, billers and services, subscription lookup, due bills on the home screen, SuperQi tradePay, and a confirm callback so a bill is never charged twice.
Payment security: safeguards to reduce fraud and prevent payments from being applied to the wrong bill or charged twice.
Receipts: a payment receipt with a QR code rendered on the phone, saved to Tasdid and shareable from the app.

Partner deeplinks: any mini-app inside SuperQi can open Tasdid+ on a specific account with a qicardwallet:// link. The parameters survive the container's re-encoding, the partner is verified server-side, and after payment a countdown sends the user back. I wrote the onboarding guide partners integrate against.

Request money: a two-step flow with a contact picker, receiving account, fee breakdown, share text, and lists of sent and received requests. It boots into its own yellow theme when launched from SuperQi's home tile.
Merchant quick invoice: a merchant account builds an itemised invoice from saved or custom services, with quantities, a note, a preview and a shareable invoice number.

Speed and resilience: lazy-loaded pages with idle prefetch, a boot splash picked before first paint, loading and error states everywhere, and a demo mode that fakes the container and the backend so the UI can be recorded without production data.

sections.heading: Keeping partner journeys connected
sections.lede: A link that survives three decode passes and comes back with the user.
sections.body: When customers arrive from another SuperQi mini-app, Tasdid+ opens the bill they came to pay instead of making them start over. After payment, it takes them back to where they began. I built the handoff and added partner checks so each app can open only the services it is allowed to use, keeping the payment on the intended path.

sections.heading: How it runs
bullets: I chose Svelte because its small JavaScript payload suits a mini-app running inside SuperQi.

Deeplink routing: the SuperQi container can change a partner link before Tasdid+ opens. I built startup routing to restore the intended destination before the first screen appears, so customers land directly on the bill they came to pay without a flash of the home screen or extra searching.
The SuperQi bridge (hylid-bridge, the Alipay+ my.* JSAPI) handles auth codes, the contact picker, the navigation bar and tradePay.
I worked with DevOps to package the mini-app in Docker and set up separate development, staging and production environments.

jabi.name: Jabi+
jabi.tagline: Bringing sales, statements and payroll into the merchant experience in SuperQi.
jabi.summary: Jabi+ is a merchant app inside SuperQi for tracking card sales, reviewing statements and paying employees. Based on merchant feedback, I added User management so merchants could bring their team into the same mini-app. I built the transaction ledger and statement export, then expanded my work into payroll and team management.

stack: Arabic with right to left layouts

sections.heading: From sales to everyday merchant work
sections.body:
A merchant taking card payments through Qi needs to see what came in, find a transaction and get an account statement. Jabi+ puts those services inside SuperQi.

I've been working on it since December 2025 as a software engineer on Qi's Billing Team. My work started with the sales pages, transaction ledger and statement export. In 2026, I added Salary for employee payments. Merchant feedback also led to User management, allowing merchants to add their team to the same mini-app.

I chose Svelte for Jabi+ because its small JavaScript payload suits a mini-app running inside SuperQi.

sections.heading: Making the sales details useful
sections.body:
I built the weekly sales view to open on today, with day tabs for the rest of the week. Each transaction brings its amount, commission, time and status together. For a closer look, I worked on the monthly ledger with date ranges, filters and totals, so a merchant can narrow the list to the entries they need.

Statements needed their own experience too. I built the pages for choosing a period, requesting a statement and returning to the generated files. A file may still be preparing, or the phone may be unable to open it. Those states have plain Arabic messages, so the page explains what happened alongside the download action.

sections.heading: Taking Salary beyond a pay button
sections.body:
Salary was a larger piece of the work. I built the employee roster, profiles and salary details, including a base amount, allowances and deductions. Merchants can find employees by name or job title and choose the people they want to pay.

Before confirming, the page brings the employee count and total together. I used a swipe for the final payment action, giving that step a deliberate confirmation. The interface also shows payment status, including when a payment needs attention.

The work continues after the payment. I built payroll records that open into each employee's result, with a reason when a payment did not go through. Each salary statement shows the base salary, allowances, deductions and net amount, with a downloadable copy. Keeping those details connected was a substantial part of my contribution.

aml.name: Staff dashboard
aml.tagline: The web app where compliance reporters review the day's anti-money-laundering alerts, investigate an account and file the case. It was two years old when I joined, and I spent four months making it easier to use.
aml.summary: I joined the project in November 2024 and worked with the team until August 2025. My contribution covered shared components, search and tables, and Arabic and English interfaces.

sections.heading: Joining the project
sections.body: The dashboard was already running when I joined. I worked from team tickets and review comments, starting with a shared component and translation work before moving on to search and table improvements.

sections.heading: Changes across pages
sections.body:
The same detail view appeared on a search page and inside a dialog. I moved it into one component used by both, so a fix could reach both places.

I also added search filters and a reset button, and kept the table's action column visible while the rest of the table scrolled.

sections.heading: Bringing the dashboard to English
sections.body:
The dashboard had been built in Arabic, so adding English meant more than translating a few labels. I used i18n to bring English across the workflow compliance staff rely on: reviewing alerts, searching accounts and investigating cases. The same screens, tables, forms and dialogs needed to work in both languages, so staff could use one consistent dashboard instead of learning a separate experience.

I carried the translations through the interface while preserving the Arabic right-to-left layout. That made English a complete option across the product, alongside the Arabic experience the team already used.

service-provider.name: Tasdid Merchant
service-provider.tagline: Tasdid Merchant lets people pay digital bills through a nearby merchant, without needing SuperQi or a bank account.
service-provider.summary: I worked on Tasdid Merchant with Qi's Billing Team. My part was making the bill lookup fit the merchant's governorate, keeping the selected provider visible and showing clear feedback when a payment was complete, still processing or unsuccessful.

sections.heading: Making digital bill payment accessible
sections.body:
Not everyone who needs to pay a digital bill has SuperQi or a bank account. Tasdid Merchant gives them another option: they can take the bill to a nearby merchant, who looks it up and pays it through the mini-app inside SuperQi.

The merchant chooses a governorate, bill category and provider, then enters the account number from the bill. Tasdid Merchant shows the customer's name, bill number and amount due so the merchant can check the details before paying. The result is recorded in the merchant's payment history.

The Arabic, right-to-left interface accepts both Arabic and Western digits for account numbers, helping merchants use it naturally while serving customers at the counter.

sections.heading: My part in the merchant experience
sections.body:
I worked on Tasdid Merchant from December 2024 to February 2025 as a Software Engineer on the Billing Team. My changes covered provider lookup, the account number step and payment feedback.

The governorate needs to carry through to the provider list. I worked on that filtering so merchants saw the providers available in the location they chose. I also kept the provider's name visible on the account number screen, so the merchant could see which provider they were looking up a bill for.

A payment still processing shouldn't look like a failed payment. I worked on separate Arabic messages for paid, processing and failed results, and on showing an error when a payment couldn't start. The point was to give the merchant a useful answer at each of those stops.

sections.heading: Supporting the work before release
sections.body:
Alongside those changes, I added Microsoft Clarity analytics and supported the builds used for testing. I worked in Svelte and TypeScript, with Vite and Tailwind CSS.

This was part of the Billing Team's work. My contribution was in the merchant interface and the feedback around bill lookup and payment, within the larger Tasdid service.

This mini-app runs inside SuperQi, so keeping its JavaScript payload small matters. Svelte was a good fit for that constraint.

sections.heading: Starting with the foundation
sections.body:
I set up Qi Hawala in January 2024. Hawala is the Arabic word for a money transfer, and the mini-app brings that task into SuperQi. People choose a Qi account, enter the recipient's details and review the amount and fee before sending. They can then return to a receipt or look through their transfer history.

The project was put on hold because of regulatory requirements and business needs. The mini-app uses Svelte to keep its JavaScript payload small inside SuperQi.

sections.heading: Designing a careful transfer flow
sections.body:
I built the transfer journey around the choices people need to make before sending money. They select a Qi account, enter the recipient's bank details, then review the amount and fee before confirming. A receipt records the outcome, and transfer history helps them find earlier transactions.

I kept the balance hidden until someone chooses to reveal it. I also kept the form options separate from the screen components, so the available choices could change without rebuilding the flow.

krg.tagline: e-Psûle lets people in the Kurdistan Region look up and pay bills from their phone inside SuperQi. I built its mini-app inside SuperQi and the staff dashboard behind it.
krg.summary: I started the mini-app in March 2025 and built the bill-payment journey, including bill lookup, payment through SuperQi, receipts, favorites and bulk payment, in Kurdish, Arabic and English. In late August, I also built the staff dashboard, where administrators manage users, roles and customers behind sign-in with Google Authenticator.

sections.heading: From finding a bill to keeping the receipt
sections.lede: I built the customer journey inside SuperQi.
sections.body:
e-Psûle is a regional bill payment service, including bills from providers such as the Ministry of Electricity. My part was the mini-app customers use inside SuperQi. I started from Qi's template and built the screens that take someone from choosing a service and entering their account number to reviewing the invoice and paying it.

The invoice needed to make the amount and dates clear before the customer continued. If a bill had expired, the app explained that at this stage. Where partial payments were available, customers could choose an amount within the allowed limits. These details were part of making the journey understandable before asking someone to pay.

sections.heading: Making the result clear
sections.body:
A payment result could be successful, pending or failed, and each needed a clear response. I kept a failed payment's invoice in view so the customer could try again. A pending payment stayed pending on screen, rather than being presented as a completed one.

I built the receipts and wrote the PDF receipt templates in all three languages, so customers could keep or share a record of their payment. I also added payment history, named favorites and bulk payments. A saved bill could be found again next month, and when several bills were paid together, the summary showed a separate result for each one.

sections.heading: Carrying three languages through the whole app
sections.body:
Kurdish, Arabic and English needed to work from the opening screen through to the receipt and help pages. I carried the language choice through the mini-app, with right to left layouts for Arabic and Sorani Kurdish and a separate typeface for Kurdish.

I also supported Arabic-Indic digits in the account field, so customers could enter an account number using the digits they normally type. The language work covered those smaller interactions as well as the text itself.

sections.heading: A second interface for staff
sections.body:
In late August 2025, I built the staff dashboard too. It served a different audience, with tables and forms for managing staff accounts and viewing customer records, in Arabic and English.

The mini-app was built with Svelte and TypeScript, whose small JavaScript payload suits an app inside SuperQi. I used React for the dashboard. Both needed a layout that followed the selected language. Together, they show the two sides of my contribution, building the journey customers see and the interface staff use to support the service.

basmayah.name: Basmayah
basmayah.tagline: Apply for a Basmayah Complex housing loan from your phone, bring a guarantor, and follow the bank's decision all the way to the keys.
basmayah.summary: Basmayah lets people apply for a housing loan for a home in Basmayah Complex through SuperQi. I built the mini-app over three days, working from the UI/UX team's designs and specifications. The work covered the application forms, documents, review screens and progress views, with Arabic and right to left layouts throughout.
basmayah.role: Software Engineer on the Billing Team

sections.heading: Making a loan application easier to follow
sections.body:
Basmayah Complex is a housing development in Baghdad. This mini-app brings the housing loan application into SuperQi, so applicants can enter their information, add documents and follow the progress from their phone.

My responsibility was the mini-app. The UI/UX team had already prepared the designs and a detailed specification. I used that work as the starting point and turned it into a working Arabic interface.

sections.heading: Building around the application
sections.body:
I divided the application into steps for personal information, documents, a guarantor and a final review. People could save a draft and return to where they left off, while the review screen brought everything together before they sent it.

Document attachments needed more than an upload button. I built previews and feedback for each attachment, including a way to retry a failed upload without picking the file again. The progress screens then explained where an application stood and when the applicant needed to do something, such as replace a document.

The whole interface was built for Arabic. I paid attention to the reading order, form layouts and the way numbers sit inside right to left text, so a phone number or reference would still read correctly.

sections.heading: How I worked within three days
sections.body:
The design work was already in place, which let me spend those three days on implementation. I started with the pieces that would appear across the app, including form fields, document cards, navigation and status views. Reusing them gave me a consistent way to build the remaining screens.

I also built with fictional sample data, so I could open the different screens and review their states without waiting for the backend or using customer information. That kept the interface work moving while I checked how the forms, feedback and navigation fit together.

I used Svelte because its small JavaScript payload suits a mini-app running inside SuperQi.

sections.heading: What I completed
sections.body:
From 9 to 11 September 2026, I completed the mini-app for the applicant and guarantor journeys. The wider product involved work across the team, and the designs and specifications came from the UI/UX team.

For me, this project shows how much a clear brief and reusable components help when time is short. The result was a connected mobile interface, from starting an application to reviewing it and following its progress.
